issues.description: The problem statement and UML refer to a Meal class (with constructor Meal(String, String[]) and getters) and expect code to use Meal. However, the provided template does not include an implemented Meal class (Meal.java is empty) and instead contains an Order class with the same structure. This name/type mismatch between Meal (expected in the specification) and Order (present in the template) will confuse students and prevent them from following the instructions that refer to Meal.
issues.suggestedFix: Provide the Meal class in the template matching the problem statement (Meal.java with a constructor Meal(String, String[]) and getters). Remove or rename the stray Order class or clearly document its presence; update example code in Main to use Meal. Ensuring the template contains Meal (not Order) will align the template with the specification and the solution.

issues.description: The problem statement and the solution refer to the core domain entity as 'Meal' (class Meal, methods taking Meal), but the template repository provides a class named 'Order' (src/de/tum/cit/ase/Order.java) instead of a Meal implementation, and the template's Meal.java file is empty. This creates a direct mapping confusion: students reading the problem expect to use/implement Meal, but the starter code exposes Order. The solution uses Meal, so the template's different identifier is likely unintentional and will force students to resolve an extra name mismatch unrelated to the learning objectives.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the template with the problem and solution by renaming or replacing the template's Order class to Meal (file and class name), and populate src/de/tum/cit/ase/Meal.java with the Meal implementation (including the same fields and getters as in the solution). Update any template references (e.g., Main) from Order to Meal. Alternatively, if Order was intended, update the problem statement to consistently use 'Order' instead of 'Meal'.
